section_summary: This section covers documents from late 1941 to late 1943 concerning motion pictures and related visual media involving Japan. In late August and early September 1941, Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and Commercial Attaché Frank S. Williams report on the critical situation facing American motion picture distributors in Japan, whose Japanese employees demanded exorbitant retirement allowances and issued threats amidst impending Japanese film monopolies and frozen assets. Later wartime records from 1943 include a Tokyo Domei broadcast report on educational slide production by Kokusai Bunka Shinkokai for Southeast Asia, an Alien Property Custodian inquiry regarding vesting orders for Japanese government-owned films in the United States, Office of War Information correspondence attempting to locate the Japanese naval film 'Our Fleet' for a Pacific War documentary, and a cross-reference noting Finnish Foreign Office reactions to the Japanese film 'Japan's Wild Eagles'.

subfiles.about: Concluding page of a diplomatic despatch from Ambassador Grew urging State Department protection for American motion picture companies facing exorbitant severance demands in Japan.
subfiles.summary: In this concluding page of Despatch No. 5824, Ambassador Joseph C. Grew urges the U.S. government to take cognizance of the plight of American motion picture companies in Japan and institute measures to protect American firms against exorbitant demands and threats. He encloses a detailed memorandum from Commercial Attaché Frank S. Williams and an oral statement presented to the Japanese Foreign Office. Copies were noted for distribution to the Department of State and the Division of Commercial Affairs.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5824 from Embassy Tokyo Regarding Protection of American Film Companies (Concluding Page)

subfiles.about: A memorandum detailing exorbitant retirement allowance demands, unauthorized meetings, and police threats made against eight American film companies in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Commercial Attaché Frank S. Williams reports that representatives of all eight American motion picture companies operating in Japan informed him of demands by their Japanese staffs for exorbitant retirement allowances in the event the companies are forced to close. The employees demanded two years' salary plus three months per year of service—exceeding one million yen in total—and rejected management's counteroffer of one month per year of service. Japanese staff held unauthorized indignation meetings, threatened managers with police detention and travel bans, and sought to claim part of eleven and a half million yen in frozen company profits, prompting Williams to urge official diplomatic representations.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Commercial Attaché Frank S. Williams on Demands Faced by American Motion Picture Companies in Japan

subfiles.about: An oral diplomatic statement lodged with the Japanese Foreign Office regarding exorbitant severance demands and threats directed at American motion picture distributors.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew delivers an oral statement to Terasaki, Chief of the American Bureau of the Japanese Foreign Office, expressing serious concern over exorbitant severance demands imposed by Japanese employees on American motion picture firms. The statement outlines the excessive financial claims totaling over one million yen, the rejection of standard severance terms, and unauthorized office meetings accompanied by threats of police detention and exit restrictions against managers. Grew formally requests that the Japanese Government intervene to protect American firms against such threats and unreasonable demands.
subfiles.title: Oral Statement Presented by Ambassador Grew to Foreign Office Bureau Chief Terasaki

subfiles.about: A monitored Domei news broadcast reporting on color picture slides produced by the Society for International Cultural Relations to promote Japanese life in southern regions.
subfiles.summary: A radio broadcast report from Tokyo Domei details that the Kokusai Bunka Shinkokai (Society for International Cultural Relations) is producing color picture slides depicting Japanese life for distribution in southern regions. Two series of 100 slides each, showing general scenes of Japan and national school activities, have been completed, with more planned. Special projection apparatus is also being manufactured, including oil-lamp projectors designed for rural southern areas without electricity.
subfiles.title: Domei English Broadcast on Educational Slide Series by Kokusai Bunka Shinkokai

subfiles.about: A cross-reference file note concerning a proposed Vesting Order by the Alien Property Custodian for Japanese government-owned motion picture films in the United States.
subfiles.summary: This State Department cross-reference file note refers to a letter dated June 5, 1943, from the Alien Property Custodian regarding motion picture films in the United States owned by the Japanese Government. The communication enclosed copies of a Report and Recommendation and a proposed Vesting Order, inquiring whether the Department of State had any objections. The original document is filed under 740.00115 P.W. Japanese Government/1.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet on Proposed Vesting Order for Japanese Government-Owned Films

subfiles.about: A letter from the Office of War Information requesting a print of the Japanese propaganda film 'Our Fleet' for use in an American documentary about the Pacific War.
subfiles.summary: Philip Dunne of the Office of War Information's Overseas Branch writes to John Begg at the State Department's Division of Cultural Relations inquiring about a two-reel Japanese film titled 'Our Fleet.' Dunne explains that he is producing a film for overseas release covering every phase of the Pacific War and that footage from 'Our Fleet' would be invaluable. He asks whether the State Department has custody of the film and if a print can be provided for screening and duplicating.
subfiles.title: Letter from Philip Dunne to John Begg Requesting Japanese Film 'Our Fleet'

subfiles.about: A response from the State Department stating that it does not hold the Japanese film 'Our Fleet' and suggesting contact with the Navy Department.
subfiles.summary: John M. Begg, Assistant Chief of the Division of Cultural Relations, replies to Philip Dunne's inquiry of August 13 regarding the Japanese motion picture 'Our Fleet.' Begg states that after checking with interested State Department divisions, no officers had knowledge of the film in their custody. He suggests that the Navy Department might possess the film and be willing to provide it for Dunne's Pacific War documentary, and expresses hope to connect during an upcoming visit to New York.
subfiles.title: Letter from John M. Begg to Philip Dunne Regarding Custody of Film 'Our Fleet'

subfiles.about: A cross-reference file note referencing a diplomatic despatch from Finland on the Finnish Foreign Office's stance toward the Japanese film 'Japan's Wild Eagles'.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet records Despatch No. 2673 dated December 13, 1943, from diplomat Robert McClintock stationed in Finland. The underlying document concerns the attitude of the Finnish Foreign Office toward the Japanese motion picture entitled 'Japan's Wild Eagles.' The original paper is filed under decimal classification 811.4061 Motion Pictures/1355.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet on Finnish Foreign Office Attitude Toward 'Japan's Wild Eagles'
